stem: Why is diffusion insufficient to meet the oxygen requirements of multi-cellular organisms like humans?
solution:
Diffusion works only where **the cell is in contact with the environment**, and in a large multi-cellular body most cells are not.

- In a **single-celled organism**, the entire surface is in contact with the surroundings, so oxygen can diffuse straight in and no special organ is needed.
- In a **multi-cellular organism**, the cells are packed in layers. Only the outermost ones touch the environment at all; the cells deep inside — in muscle, in bone, in the brain — are many layers away from any surface.

Diffusion is also **far too slow** over such distances, and a human's oxygen demand is high and constant. Waiting for oxygen to diffuse from the skin to a heart muscle cell would leave that cell without oxygen for far too long.

This is exactly why humans have a **respiratory system** to take oxygen in at one place and a **transport system** — blood carrying haemoglobin — to deliver it to every cell.
groundedIn: §5.1 What are Life Processes?, which states that in multi-cellular organisms all the cells may not be in direct contact with the surrounding environment and that simple diffusion will not meet the requirements of all the cells, creating the need for a transportation system.

stem: What criteria do we use to decide whether something is alive?
solution:
**Movement of some kind** is the everyday criterion — a dog running, a plant growing — but the book shows it is not enough on its own: a plant that is not visibly growing is still alive, and some animals breathe without visible movement.

The criterion that survives is **molecular movement**. Living organisms are highly organised structures whose order is constantly liable to break down because of the environment, so they must keep **repairing and maintaining** themselves — and since those structures are made of molecules, they must be moving molecules around all the time.

So the test is the presence of the **life processes** that do this maintenance work: nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion. Viruses are the interesting case: they show no molecular movement until they infect a cell, which is partly why there is a controversy about whether they are truly alive.
groundedIn: §5.1 What are Life Processes?, which rejects visible movement as the defining characteristic, argues for invisible molecular movement, and names the maintenance processes as the life processes.

stem: What are outside raw materials used for by an organism?
solution:
Raw materials taken in from outside are used for three things:

- **Energy.** Food is the source of energy that drives every maintenance process. Because life on earth depends on carbon-based molecules, most food sources are carbon-based too.
- **Growth.** If the body size of the organism is to increase, additional raw material is needed from outside to build new tissue.
- **Repair and maintenance.** The ordered structure of a living body keeps breaking down and must constantly be repaired, which uses up materials.

Besides food, organisms take in **oxygen** for breaking food down, and plants take up **water and minerals** — nitrogen, phosphorus, iron and magnesium — from the soil for building proteins and other compounds.
groundedIn: §5.1 What are Life Processes? (energy, growth, repair, and the intake of oxygen) with §5.2.1 Autotrophic Nutrition, which lists the minerals plants take from the soil and notes that nitrogen is essential for synthesising proteins.

stem: What processes would you consider essential for maintaining life?
solution:
Four, and the book introduces them in this order because each one creates the need for the next:

- **Nutrition** — transferring a source of energy from outside the body to the inside.
- **Respiration** — acquiring oxygen and using it to break food down for cellular needs.
- **Transportation** — carrying food and oxygen from the one place they are taken in to every part of the body that needs them.
- **Excretion** — removing the harmful by-products that energy generation creates.

In a single-celled organism no special organs are needed for any of these, because the whole surface is in contact with the environment. It is the **increase in body size and complexity** that forces specialised tissues, and with them the need for transport.
groundedIn: §5.1 What are Life Processes?, which introduces nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion in turn, each arising from the limits of the one before.

stem: What are the differences between autotrophic nutrition and heterotrophic nutrition?
solution:
| Basis | Autotrophic nutrition | Heterotrophic nutrition |
|---|---|---|
| **Food source** | Simple inorganic substances — carbon dioxide and water | Complex organic substances made by other organisms |
| **Food making** | The organism **makes its own** food | The organism **cannot** make its own food |
| **Chlorophyll** | Present, and necessary | Absent |
| **Sunlight** | Required | Not required |
| **Enzymes** | Not needed to break food down first | **Bio-catalysts called enzymes** break the complex food into simpler forms |
| **Examples** | Green plants and some bacteria | Animals and fungi |

The dependence runs one way: the survival of heterotrophs depends, **directly or indirectly, on autotrophs**.
groundedIn: §5.2 Nutrition, which distinguishes autotrophs using inorganic carbon dioxide and water from heterotrophs using complex substances broken down by enzymes, and states that heterotroph survival depends directly or indirectly on autotrophs.

stem: Where do plants get each of the raw materials required for photosynthesis?
solution:
- **Carbon dioxide** — from the **air**, entering the leaf through the **stomata**.
- **Water** — from the **soil**, taken up by the **roots** in terrestrial plants and carried to the leaves in the xylem.
- **Sunlight** — from the **sun**, absorbed by the **chlorophyll** in the leaves.
- **Minerals** — from the **soil**: nitrogen, phosphorus, iron and magnesium. Nitrogen is essential for synthesising proteins and other compounds, and is taken up either as inorganic **nitrates or nitrites**, or as organic compounds that **bacteria** have prepared from atmospheric nitrogen.
groundedIn: §5.2.1 Autotrophic Nutrition, which names carbon dioxide, water, sunlight and chlorophyll as what photosynthesis converts and takes, and lists the soil minerals with the two routes by which nitrogen is taken up; Fig. 5.3 for the stomatal pore.

stem: What is the role of the acid in our stomach?
solution:
The **gastric glands** in the wall of the stomach release hydrochloric acid, and it does two jobs:

- It **creates an acidic medium which facilitates the action of the enzyme pepsin**, the protein-digesting enzyme released alongside it. Pepsin cannot work except in acid.
- It **kills the bacteria** that enter with the food, so they do not reach the intestine alive.

The stomach protects itself from its own acid with **mucus**, also released by the gastric glands, which coats and shields the inner lining.
groundedIn: §5.2.4 Nutrition in Human Beings, which records that the gastric glands release hydrochloric acid, pepsin and mucus, that the acid creates the acidic medium pepsin needs, and asks what other function the acid serves.

stem: What is the function of digestive enzymes?
solution:
Digestive enzymes are **biological catalysts that break complex food molecules down into simpler ones** small enough to be absorbed from the alimentary canal into the blood.

Each acts on one class of food:

- **Salivary amylase**, in saliva, breaks **starch** down to simple sugar.
- **Pepsin**, in the stomach, digests **proteins** — and needs the acid medium the hydrochloric acid provides.
- **Trypsin**, from the pancreas, digests **proteins**; **lipase**, also from the pancreas, breaks down **emulsified fats**.
- The enzymes of the **intestinal juice** finish the job, converting proteins to **amino acids**, complex carbohydrates to **glucose**, and fats to **fatty acids and glycerol**.
groundedIn: §5.2.4 Nutrition in Human Beings, which names the enzymes as biological catalysts and traces salivary amylase, pepsin, trypsin, lipase and the intestinal enzymes with the final products of each.

stem: How is the small intestine designed to absorb digested food?
solution:
By making its absorbing surface as large as possible and putting blood right behind it.

- The small intestine is the **longest part of the alimentary canal**, fitted into a compact space by extensive **coiling**.
- Its inner lining carries **numerous finger-like projections called villi**, which **increase the surface area for absorption** enormously.
- The villi are **richly supplied with blood vessels**, so absorbed food passes straight into the blood and is carried to every cell of the body — for energy, for building new tissue and for repairing old tissue.

The same principle appears elsewhere in the chapter: the alveoli enlarge the surface for gas exchange in exactly this way.
groundedIn: §5.2.4 Nutrition in Human Beings, which describes the coiling of the small intestine, the villi that increase the surface area for absorption and their rich blood supply.

stem: What advantage over an aquatic organism does a terrestrial organism have with regard to obtaining oxygen for respiration?
solution:
A terrestrial organism breathes the **oxygen in the atmosphere**, which is far richer in oxygen than water is. An aquatic organism must use the **oxygen dissolved in water**, and there is much less of it.

Two consequences follow:

- A terrestrial organism obtains the oxygen it needs with **much less effort**.
- An aquatic organism has to push a **large volume of water** past its gills to collect enough, which is why the **rate of breathing in aquatic organisms is much faster** than in terrestrial ones. A fish takes water in through its mouth and forces it past the gills, where the dissolved oxygen is taken up by the blood.
groundedIn: §5.3 Respiration, which states that terrestrial animals breathe atmospheric oxygen while animals living in water use dissolved oxygen, and that the rate of breathing in aquatic organisms is much faster; Activity 5.6 and the fish-gill description.

stem: What are the different ways in which glucose is oxidised to provide energy in various organisms?
solution:
Every pathway begins the same way and then forks.

**Step common to all.** Glucose, a **six-carbon** molecule, is broken down in the **cytoplasm** into **pyruvate**, a **three-carbon** molecule.

Pyruvate is then dealt with in one of three ways:

**1. Anaerobic respiration — in yeast, during fermentation.** In the **absence of oxygen**, pyruvate is converted in the cytoplasm into **ethanol and carbon dioxide**.

**2. Aerobic respiration — in most organisms.** In the **presence of oxygen**, pyruvate is broken down in the **mitochondria** into **three molecules of carbon dioxide and water**. The energy released here is **a lot greater** than in the anaerobic pathway.

**3. Lack of oxygen — in our muscle cells.** During sudden activity, when oxygen runs short, pyruvate is converted into **lactic acid**, also a three-carbon molecule. Its build-up in the muscles is what causes **cramps**.

In every case the energy released is immediately used to make **ATP**, the energy currency that fuels all other activities in the cell.
groundedIn: §5.3 Respiration with Fig. 5.8, which sets out the three break-down pathways from pyruvate and their locations, and the ATP note in the same section.

stem: How is oxygen and carbon dioxide transported in human beings?
solution:
The two gases are carried in **different ways**, because they differ in how readily they dissolve in blood.

**Oxygen — carried by a respiratory pigment.** Diffusion alone cannot deliver oxygen throughout a body as large as ours. Oxygen is therefore picked up in the alveoli by **haemoglobin**, the respiratory pigment present in the **red blood corpuscles**, which has a **very high affinity for oxygen**. It carries the oxygen to tissues that are deficient in it and releases it there.

**Carbon dioxide — carried dissolved.** Carbon dioxide is **more soluble in water than oxygen is**, so it needs no pigment: it is mostly transported in the **dissolved form in the blood**, back to the lungs for release into the alveoli.
groundedIn: §5.3 Respiration, which names haemoglobin as the respiratory pigment in the red blood corpuscles with a very high affinity for oxygen, and states that carbon dioxide is more soluble and mostly transported dissolved.

stem: How are the lungs designed in human beings to maximise the area for exchange of gases?
solution:
By dividing the air passage until it ends in an enormous number of tiny sacs.

- Within the lungs the passage **divides into smaller and smaller tubes**, which finally terminate in balloon-like structures called **alveoli**.
- The alveoli **provide the surface where the exchange of gases takes place**. Being very numerous and very small, together they present a huge area in a small volume.
- The walls of the alveoli contain an **extensive network of blood vessels**, so the blood is brought into the closest possible contact with the air.

Breathing keeps that surface supplied: lifting the ribs and flattening the diaphragm enlarges the chest cavity and sucks air into the expanded alveoli. The lungs also retain a **residual volume of air**, so there is sufficient time for oxygen to be absorbed and carbon dioxide released.
groundedIn: §5.3 Respiration with Fig. 5.9, which describes the branching passage ending in alveoli, their extensive network of blood vessels, the breathing mechanism and the residual volume of air.

stem: What are the components of the transport system in human beings? What are the functions of these components?
solution:
The circulatory system has **three components**, plus a fourth fluid alongside it.

**1. The heart.** A muscular organ about the size of our fist, with **four chambers** so that oxygen-rich blood never mixes with carbon dioxide-rich blood. It pumps de-oxygenated blood to the lungs and oxygenated blood to the rest of the body.

**2. Blood.** The fluid that does the carrying — oxygen, carbon dioxide, digested food, and excretory products. It carries **platelet cells**, which plug leaks by clotting the blood at a point of injury.

**3. Blood vessels.**

- **Arteries** carry blood **away from** the heart. Because blood leaves the heart under high pressure, they have **thick, elastic walls**.
- **Veins** bring blood **back to** the heart. The blood is no longer under pressure, so they need no thick walls, but they have **valves** that keep blood flowing in one direction only.
- **Capillaries**, into which arteries divide inside an organ, are where exchange with the tissues happens.

**4. Lymph.** Plasma, proteins and blood cells that escape through the capillary walls form this tissue fluid. It **carries digested and absorbed fat from the intestine** and **drains excess fluid** from the extracellular space back into the blood.
groundedIn: §5.4.1 Transportation in Human Beings with Fig. 5.10 and Fig. 5.11 — the heart and its chambers, arteries and veins with their wall thickness and valves, platelets, and the lymph paragraph that follows.

stem: Why is it necessary to separate oxygenated and deoxygenated blood in mammals and birds?
solution:
Because mammals and birds have **high energy needs**, and keeping the two streams apart is what allows a **highly efficient supply of oxygen to the body**.

Both are **warm-blooded**: they constantly use energy to **maintain their body temperature**, whatever the temperature outside. That demands a steady, generous supply of oxygen, because aerobic respiration is what releases the energy. If oxygenated blood mixed with de-oxygenated blood, the blood pumped to the body would carry **less oxygen per unit volume**, and the supply would fall short.

The contrast makes the point:

- **Amphibians and many reptiles** do not use energy to keep their body temperature up — it simply follows the environment. They manage with **three-chambered hearts** and tolerate some mixing.
- **Fishes** have only **two chambers**; blood passes through the heart once per cycle.

The four-chambered heart of mammals and birds separates the streams completely.
groundedIn: §5.4.1 Transportation in Human Beings, which states that the separation allows a highly efficient supply of oxygen, useful in animals with high energy needs such as birds and mammals that constantly use energy to maintain body temperature, and contrasts the three- and two-chambered hearts.

stem: What are the components of the transport system in highly organised plants?
solution:
Plants have **two independently organised conducting tubes**, together making up the **vascular tissue**:

- **Xylem** — moves **water and minerals** taken up from the soil, upward from the roots to the rest of the plant. Its vessels and tracheids interconnect to form a continuous system of water-conducting channels reaching all parts of the plant.
- **Phloem** — transports the **products of photosynthesis** from the leaves where they are made to wherever they are needed, along with amino acids and other substances.

The two pathways are separate by design, because they carry different things in different directions.
groundedIn: §5.4.2 Transportation in Plants, which names xylem and phloem as two independently organised conducting tubes and states what each moves.

stem: How are water and minerals transported in plants?
solution:
In the **xylem**, whose vessels and tracheids in root, stem and leaf interconnect into a continuous channel reaching every part of the plant. **Two forces** move the water up it, and they matter at different times.

**1. Root pressure.** Cells of the root in contact with the soil **actively take up ions**. This creates a difference in ion concentration between root and soil, so water moves into the root from the soil to eliminate that difference. The result is a steady movement of water into the root xylem, creating a **column of water that is steadily pushed upwards**.

**2. Transpiration pull.** Root pressure alone is **unlikely to be enough** for the heights plants commonly reach. Water evaporating from the cells of a leaf — lost as vapour through the stomata, which is **transpiration** — creates a **suction that pulls water up from the xylem cells of the roots**.

**Which force dominates, and when.** Root pressure matters most **at night**. During the **day**, when the stomata are open, the **transpiration pull is the major driving force**. Transpiration also helps in temperature regulation.
groundedIn: §5.4.2 Transportation in Plants with Activity 5.8 and Fig. 5.12 — the continuous xylem channels, active ion uptake creating root pressure, the transpiration pull and the statement that root pressure matters more at night while transpiration pull dominates by day.

stem: How is food transported in plants?
solution:
By **translocation** in the **phloem**.

**Translocation** is the transport of the soluble products of photosynthesis from the leaves, where they are formed, to the rest of the plant. Besides those products the phloem also carries **amino acids and other substances**.

- It takes place in the **sieve tubes**, helped by the **adjacent companion cells**.
- It moves in **both upward and downward directions** — unlike the xylem, whose flow is one way.
- The material is delivered especially to the **storage organs** of roots, fruits and seeds, and to **growing organs**.

Transport in xylem is largely explained by simple physical forces; translocation in phloem is **achieved by utilising energy**.
groundedIn: §5.4.2 Transportation in Plants, under Transport of food and other substances, which defines translocation, names the sieve tubes and companion cells, gives the two-way movement and the destinations, and contrasts it with the physical forces moving xylem sap.

stem: Describe the structure and functioning of nephrons.
solution:
**A nephron is the basic filtration unit of the kidney.** Each kidney has large numbers of them packed close together.

**Structure.** Each nephron has:

- A **cluster of very thin-walled blood capillaries**, supplied by a branch of the renal artery.
- A **cup-shaped end of a coiled tube called Bowman's capsule**, which surrounds that capillary cluster and collects the filtrate.
- The **coiled tube** itself, which leads away from the capsule.

**Functioning.**

1. **Filtration.** Blood is filtered through the thin walls of the capillary cluster, and the filtrate — containing nitrogenous wastes such as **urea and uric acid**, and also useful substances — is collected by Bowman's capsule.
2. **Selective re-absorption.** As the filtrate flows along the tube, useful substances are taken back into the blood: **glucose, amino acids, salts and a major amount of water**. How much water is re-absorbed depends on **how much excess water there is in the body** and **how much dissolved waste there is to excrete**.
3. **Collection.** What remains is **urine**, which enters the **ureter** and passes to the urinary bladder.

The scale of the re-absorption is the striking part: in a healthy adult the initial filtrate is about **180 L daily**, while only **a litre or two** is actually excreted.
groundedIn: §5.5.1 Excretion in Human Beings with Fig. 5.13 and Fig. 5.14 — the capillary cluster, Bowman's capsule, selective re-absorption of glucose, amino acids, salts and water, and the 180 L figure in the artificial-kidney note.

stem: What are the methods used by plants to get rid of excretory products?
solution:
Plants use **completely different strategies** from animals, and can afford to, because many of their tissues consist of dead cells and they can lose parts of themselves.

- **Gaseous wastes** — oxygen from photosynthesis and carbon dioxide from respiration are released by **diffusion through the stomata**.
- **Excess water** — got rid of by **transpiration**.
- **Stored in vacuoles** — many plant waste products are stored in **cellular vacuoles**.
- **Stored in leaves that fall off** — waste goes with the leaf when it is shed.
- **Stored as resins and gums** — especially in **old xylem**, which is dead tissue.
- **Excreted into the soil** — some waste substances are passed out into the soil around the plant.

Oxygen is worth noticing here: it is itself a **waste product** of photosynthesis.
groundedIn: §5.5.2 Excretion in Plants, which lists transpiration, cellular vacuoles, fallen leaves, resins and gums in old xylem, and excretion into the surrounding soil, and points out that oxygen can be thought of as a waste product of photosynthesis.

stem: How is the amount of urine produced regulated?
solution:
By how much water the nephron **re-absorbs** from the filtrate as it flows along the tubule. Two things decide that:

- **How much excess water there is in the body.** If the body has water to spare, less is re-absorbed and the urine is more dilute and greater in volume; if the body is short of water, more is re-absorbed and the urine is scanty and concentrated.
- **How much dissolved waste there is to be excreted.** More waste needs more water to carry it out.

The margin available is enormous: the initial filtrate in a healthy adult is about **180 L a day**, and only **a litre or two** leaves the body, because the rest is re-absorbed in the kidney tubules.
groundedIn: §5.5.1 Excretion in Human Beings, which states that the amount of water re-absorbed depends on how much excess water there is in the body and how much dissolved waste there is to be excreted, with the 180 L figure from the artificial-kidney note.
